title: The Volkswagen Emissions Scandal Explained Like You're 5
hook: Eleven million cars, built by one company, broke the law every time they started, and passed every official test anyway -- because the engine always knew when it was being watched.
body:
Volkswagen began selling its 'Clean Diesel' TDI engines in the United States starting with the 2009 model year, marketing them as fuel-efficient and low-emission. To pass America's strict nitrogen-oxide tests while still hitting the mileage and power Volkswagen had promised, engineers built 'defeat device' software into the engine computer, which could detect a lab test (using signals including steering-wheel position, speed and drive-cycle length -- sharpened around April 2013) and switch on full pollution controls only then. On the road, the cars emitted nitrogen oxide at up to 40 times the legal US limit. In 2013 the nonprofit International Council on Clean Transportation gave West Virginia University a $69,000 grant to road-test diesel emissions; in May 2014, WVU researchers drove a VW Jetta, a VW Passat and a BMW (as a control) roughly 1,300 miles and found the BMW clean but the two Volkswagens failing by 15 to 40 times the legal limit. After more than a year of being pressed by CARB and the EPA, Volkswagen's own engineers admitted on September 3, 2015 that the cars held a defeat device. The EPA issued a public Notice of Violation on September 18, 2015; EPA enforcement chief Cynthia Giles called it 'a threat to public health.' VW America CEO Michael Horn publicly apologized on September 21 ('we have totally screwed up'), and testified before Congress on October 8 that the device 'was installed for this purpose.' CEO Martin Winterkorn resigned September 23, 2015, saying he was 'not aware of any wrongdoing' on his part. Volkswagen ultimately admitted roughly 11 million affected vehicles worldwide (about 590,000 in the US). In October 2016 a federal judge approved a $14.7 billion settlement, at the time the largest auto-scandal settlement in US history. VW engineer James Liang pleaded guilty in September 2016 (sentenced to 40 months, August 2017); compliance manager Oliver Schmidt was arrested by the FBI in Miami in January 2017 and later sentenced to 7 years (December 2017). In January 2017 Volkswagen agreed to plead guilty to three federal felony counts and pay $4.3 billion; the firm formally entered its guilty plea in Detroit in March 2017. In May 2018 a US grand jury indicted Martin Winterkorn on conspiracy and wire-fraud counts, but Germany does not extradite its own citizens, and he was never tried in the US. Audi CEO Rupert Stadler was arrested in Germany in June 2018 and pleaded guilty in Munich in June 2023 (suspended sentence, $1.2 million fine). Winterkorn's own German trial finally opened in Braunschweig on September 3, 2024 -- nine years after he resigned -- and was later suspended over his health, with no verdict reached in the record this account was built from. In May 2025 the same court convicted two other former VW managers, Jens Hadler (4 years 6 months) and Hanno Jelden (2 years 7 months). By 2020 Volkswagen itself put the scandal's worldwide cost at more than 31.3 billion euros, roughly $34.7 billion. This is what the EPA's Notice of Violation, the DOJ's 2017 plea agreement, and contemporaneous reporting say happened.

Every figure used is checked against a source in the production notes (docs/research/volkswagen_dieselgate.md).

For educational and entertainment purposes. Historical events are dramatised; no dialogue in this video is presented as a verbatim quotation except where directly attributed on screen.

pinned: The part that still gets me: every regulator tested these cars for years and passed them every time. It took three ordinary cars on ordinary roads -- funded by a $69,000 grant -- to catch what a decade of official labs never did. Where would you have caught it first?
